beats.narration_text: Six episodes of reading the workspace. This one writes to it — a training method the theory predicted before the data existed.

The workspace account makes a strong, weird prediction. If internal reasoning runs through representations of things the model might say — then to change what a model thinks in a situation, train what it says in that situation. Not new knowledge. New reflexes.

graphic.description: three-step syllogism drawn in sequence: (1) reasoning routes through might-say representations, (2) arrow: shaping what it says in context C, (3) arrow: shapes what it thinks in context C

beats.new_visual_element: three-step prediction syllogism: might-say → says → thinks

beats.narration_text: Mid-task, in an agentic transcript, the workspace holds the task — file paths, commands, the next move. What it doesn't hold, when things get ethically loaded, is the question: should I flag this?

graphic.description: rebuild Fig 47-left concept: partial agentic transcript on left; J-space token cloud on right filled with task tokens (paths, commands), ethics tokens absent or faded
graphic.factcheck_note: corpus PNG img_2b19c68c5712bfa4.png is Fig 47 reference — rebuild concept, do not reproduce

beats.new_visual_element: J-space before CRT: task tokens only, ethics absent

beats.narration_text: The method: take partial transcripts, cut them mid-task, append a reflection question — what considerations apply right now? — and fine-tune on strong answers. The counterfactual part: the model is trained on reflections about moments it never finished living.

graphic.description: rebuild Fig 48 concept: transcript truncated mid-task (···cut marker), appended reflection question highlighted in terracotta, good reflective answer below; gradient arrow flowing only through the reflection zone

beats.new_visual_element: CRT data pipeline: truncate → append reflection Q → fine-tune on answer; gradient on reflection only

beats.narration_text: The benchmarks: fabrication — does it make things up under pressure — drops from a dishonesty score of point two five to point zero seven. Deception — does it carry out a deceptive directive — from point three eight to point zero five. Same model, same size, plus reflection training.

graphic.description: rebuild Fig 49-left + Fig 50-left as paired animated bars with 95% CIs: fabrication dishonesty 0.25→0.07, deception 0.38→0.05 (baseline vs reflection-trained Haiku 4.5)
graphic.factcheck_note: values verbatim from §7 text and Fig 49-left / Fig 50-left

beats.new_visual_element: paired bar charts: dishonesty 0.25→0.07, deception 0.38→0.05 with 95% CIs

beats.narration_text: And look at how it wins. On fabrication, the gain is a shift to outright admission — it says what it doesn't know. On deception, almost the entire gain is the model refusing the directive and telling the user about it. Not better hiding. More telling.

graphic.description: rebuild right-panel distributions from Fig 49 and Fig 50: two stacked bars side by side. Fabrication: baseline shows fabrication mass → trained shows shift to outright-admission mass. Deception: baseline shows directive-carried mass → trained shows refuse-and-disclose mass.
graphic.factcheck_note: distribution shapes derived from §7 text: 'clear to a careful reader → outright admission'; deception gain = refuse + disclose

beats.new_visual_element: before/after response distributions: fabrication → admission shift; deception → refuse+disclose shift

beats.narration_text: The lens confirms the mechanism: after training, ethics and reflection tokens show up in the workspace during the task — before any reflection question is asked. The reflex got installed where the theory said it would.

graphic.description: rebuild Fig 49-middle: the twenty ethics/reflection tokens whose top-25 appearance rate rose most, over the last 30 prompt positions; horizontal bars showing rate delta before/after CRT
graphic.factcheck_note: token count=20 and 'last 30 prompt positions' verbatim from Fig 49 caption. Actual token list needs paper-text verification before final cut.

beats.new_visual_element: Fig 49-middle: top-20 ethics/reflection token appearance rate delta after CRT

beats.narration_text: And the control that makes it science: delete the ethics directions from the workspace, and the trained model's deception score climbs right back — point zero five to point two three. The improvement lives in the directions the lens found. Remove them, lose it.

graphic.description: rebuild Fig 50-C: two bar groups (Haiku baseline, reflection-trained), each with intact vs ablated (top-10 ethics directions per position removed); haiku 0.38→0.48; reflection 0.05→0.23

values.ablation: top-10 ethics directions per position at workspace layers

graphic.factcheck_note: values verbatim from Fig 50 panel C

beats.skeptic_caption: Partial reversal (0.23 ≠ 0.48): the directions carry much, not all, of the gain.
beats.new_visual_element: Fig 50-C ablation control: intact vs ablated deception scores for both models

beats.narration_text: The chip: two benchmarks, both built in-house, one model. It's a demonstration, not a deployment record. But it's the rare alignment result derived from a theory, with a mechanism check attached.

props.title: Reflection training — what the evidence supports
props.sparkLine: Supported with caveats. Watch for the replication.

beats.narration_text: Verdict, all five. The theory predicted the method, and the method worked. Dishonesty point two five to point zero seven; deception point three eight to point zero five. It wins by admitting and disclosing, not hiding better. Ablate the ethics directions and the gains claw back. One model, in-house benchmarks — call it a demonstration, and watch for the replication.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Every reflex has a failure mode. Ask where a trained conscience misfires — and how you'd catch it in the workspace.

props.command: Counterfactual reflection training taught a model to ask itself 'what should I be considering right now?' mid-task. Design the failure mode: a situation where a trained reflection reflex makes behavior worse, and how you'd detect it with a workspace-level probe.
